intro.why: Real problems rarely match the textbook setting: rewards are hard to write, demonstrations exist, several agents interact, and safety constraints matter. These extensions keep the sequential-decision core but change the supervision, the number of decision makers or the rules for acting.
prereq: Sessions M11–M12 (policy gradients, PPO, preference models)

sections.title: Behavioural cloning
sections.plain: Treat imitation as supervised learning: predict the expert's action from the state.
sections.body:
The standard setting assumed a given reward and free interaction. Often we instead have expert demonstrations. Behavioural cloning (BC) fits a policy to expert (state, action) pairs:

$$\mathcal L_{\text{BC}}(\theta) = -\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\log\pi_\theta(a_i^E\mid s_i)$$

Worked. If the policy gives the demonstrated action probability 0.8, the loss is −log 0.8 = 0.223; at probability 0.2 it is −log 0.2 = 1.609. Training pushes probability toward the expert's action.

BC needs no reward and no environment interaction during training, and works well with plenty of data covering the states the policy will meet.

sections.title: Distribution shift and DAgger
sections.plain: The cloned policy drifts into states the expert never showed, then makes bigger mistakes; DAgger asks the expert about those states.
sections.body:
Distribution shift. A policy affects its own future inputs. A small steering error moves the car into a state rare in the expert data, where the policy is more likely to err again, compounding away from the demonstrations. Good supervised accuracy on expert states does not guarantee good rollouts; errors can grow quadratically with the horizon.

DAgger (dataset aggregation)
  1. Train π₁ on expert demonstrations D.
  2. For i = 1, 2, …: run πᵢ (possibly mixed with the expert) to collect the states it visits; ask the expert to label the correct action in those states; add them to D; train πᵢ₊₁ on all of D.

The policy learns how to recover from its own mistakes. In ex1 (lane keeping; the expert's demonstrations stay within ±0.5 of the centre), the cloned policy is off the road 12.5% of the time; after one DAgger iteration, 0%.

sections.title: Inverse RL, maximum-entropy IRL and GAIL
sections.plain: Infer what the expert is trying to achieve, then optimise that.
sections.body:
Copying actions is not always right: two experts may take different paths with the same intent, and actions don't transfer when dynamics change. Inverse RL infers a reward under which the expert's behaviour is (near-)optimal, often linear in features, $r_w(s,a) = w^\top f(s,a)$, then solves the forward RL problem.

Non-uniqueness. Many rewards explain the same behaviour (any positive rescaling preserves the ordering; the zero reward makes every policy optimal; states never visited are unconstrained), so the goal is a useful behavioural model, not "the one true reward".

  • Maximum-entropy IRL: model the expert as giving trajectories probability ∝ exp(R(τ)), so higher-reward trajectories are exponentially more likely while several plausible ones keep probability; choose w to maximise the demonstrations' likelihood.
  • GAIL: skip an explicit reward; a discriminator learns to tell expert from learner state–action pairs and the policy is trained (with RL) to fool it, matching the expert's occupancy measure.

sections.title: Learning rewards from preferences
sections.plain: People find it easier to say which of two behaviours is better than to write a reward.
sections.body:
Human knowledge can enter as demonstrations, corrections, scalar evaluations or preferences. A reward model learns from comparisons of trajectory segments:

$$P(\tau_A \succ \tau_B) = \sigma\big(R_\phi(\tau_A) - R_\phi(\tau_B)\big),\qquad R_\phi(\tau) = \sum_t r_\phi(s_t,a_t)$$

The policy is then optimised against $r_\phi$ with ordinary RL, and new comparisons are requested on the agent's latest behaviour (active, iterative). This is how agents learned backflips from a few hundred human comparisons, and the basis of RLHF for language models (M12).

sections.title: Multi-agent RL and its challenges
sections.plain: Several learners share a world; each one's environment keeps changing as the others learn.
sections.body:
A Markov game $(\mathcal S, \{\mathcal A_i\}, P, \{R_i\}, \gamma)$ replaces the MDP: the next state and each agent's reward depend on the joint action. Settings can be cooperative (shared reward), competitive (zero-sum) or mixed.

  • Non-stationarity: from each agent's view, the environment includes other learners whose policies keep changing, breaking the Markov/stationarity assumptions behind single-agent convergence results.
  • Joint-action growth: $m^n$ joint actions for n agents with m actions each (5 actions, 8 agents: 390,625).
  • Credit assignment: a shared team reward hides which agent helped.
  • Partial observability: each agent sees only local observations.

Treating others as part of the environment (independent learners) is simple but can be unstable.

sections.title: Centralised training, decentralised execution
sections.plain: Use everyone's information while training, but let each agent act on its own view.
sections.body:
The dominant design: during training, a centralised critic (or value) uses joint observations and actions, which restores stationarity for the critic and helps credit assignment; at execution, each agent acts from its local observation only.

  • MADDPG: per-agent deterministic actors, centralised Q-critics that see all agents' observations and actions; continuous actions, cooperative or competitive.
  • QMIX: per-agent Q-values combined into a team Q-value by a monotonic mixing network, so each agent's greedy action is consistent with the joint greedy action; cooperative, discrete.
  • MAPPO: PPO with decentralised policies and a centralised value function; a strong, simple baseline.

sections.title: Safe RL with constraints
sections.plain: High reward is not the same as permitted behaviour: optimise reward subject to a cost budget.
sections.body:
$$\max_\theta J_R(\theta)\quad\text{subject to}\quad J_C(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}\Big[\sum_t\gamma^tc_t\Big] \le d$$

Costs capture collisions, energy limits or entering hazardous regions (a constrained MDP). Mechanisms: Lagrangian methods (optimise $J_R - \lambda(J_C - d)$; increase λ while the constraint is violated), constrained policy optimisation (trust-region updates that respect the constraint), action shielding (a safety layer overrides unsafe actions), and human intervention.

In ex2 (three actions with reward/cost (1.0, 0.9), (0.6, 0.3), (0.2, 0)), the Lagrangian policy first chases reward and violates the budget d = 0.3 while λ grows, then settles on the second action exactly at the budget (reward 0.6), the true constrained optimum.

Reporting safety. High average reward is not evidence of safety. Report violation rates (including during training), worst-case and tail outcomes, intervention frequency, and behaviour under distribution shift.

sections.title: Applications and reward hacking
sections.plain: RL helps when today's action changes tomorrow's options; whatever you optimise, the agent will exploit.
sections.body:
RL fits problems with repeated decisions whose current action changes future opportunities: robotics, autonomous driving, energy and grid control, data-centre cooling, recommenders, finance and trading, chip placement, and language-model post-training and agents (tokens, tool calls or code edits as actions).

Proxy rewards. A learned reward or automatic verifier is only a proxy. If the policy can score well by exploiting the test harness (editing tests, looping for respawning bonuses, verbose or flattering answers), optimisation succeeds numerically while the real task fails. Evaluate with measures beyond the training reward, hold out evaluators the agent can't influence, and inspect behaviour, not just scores.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset without interaction; it must avoid over-estimating actions not covered by the data (conservative Q-learning, implicit Q-learning).
  • Sim-to-real: domain randomisation trains on many simulated variations so the real world looks like just another variation.
  • Game theory: in competitive MARL the right solution concept may be a Nash equilibrium rather than a single optimal policy; self-play with populations (league training) helps avoid cycles.
  • Human-in-the-loop data are expensive; active querying of the most informative comparisons reduces cost.

code.title: Behavioural cloning vs DAgger on lane keeping
code.explain: Fits a lookup-table policy to expert demonstrations near the lane centre, measures how often it leaves the road, then runs five DAgger iterations in which the expert labels states the learner visits.
mistakes: Evaluating BC only on expert states.
Forgetting to aggregate data across DAgger iterations.
code.notes: The cloned policy fails because unseen offsets default to 'go straight'; DAgger fills exactly those gaps.
code.code:
"""Behavioural cloning vs DAgger on a lane-keeping task with compounding errors.

State: lateral offset x (lane centre 0). Expert steers u* = -0.5x. Dynamics: x' = x + u + noise.
The learner is a lookup table over 21 offset bins (a classifier over 5 steering actions); bins the
expert never visited default to 'go straight'. Expert demonstrations stay near the centre, so BC
has no idea what to do once it drifts; DAgger asks the expert to label states the learner visits.
"""
import numpy as np
print("BC loss at p(expert action)=0.8:", round(-np.log(0.8), 3), " at 0.2:", round(-np.log(0.2), 3))
ACTS = np.array([-1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0])
BINS = np.linspace(-3, 3, 21)
b = lambda x: int(np.argmin(np.abs(BINS - x)))
expert = lambda x: int(np.argmin(np.abs(ACTS - (-0.5 * x))))
def rollout(policy, rng, T=60, noise=0.25):
    x, xs, off = 0.0, [], 0
    for _ in range(T):
        xs.append(x); x = x + ACTS[policy(x)] + rng.normal(0, noise)
        off += abs(x) > 2.0
    return xs, off / T
def fit(data):
    counts = np.zeros((21, 5))
    for x, a in data: counts[b(x), a] += 1
    table = np.where(counts.sum(1) > 0, counts.argmax(1), 2)            # unseen bins -> go straight
    return lambda x: int(table[b(x)])
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
demos = []
for _ in range(5):                                                       # expert demonstrations (tiny expert noise)
    xs, _ = rollout(expert, rng, noise=0.05); demos += [(x, expert(x)) for x in xs]
bc = fit(demos)
print(f"expert data cover offsets {min(x for x, _ in demos):+.2f} .. {max(x for x, _ in demos):+.2f}")
test = np.random.default_rng(1)
print(f"BC:      fraction of time off the road (|x| > 2) = {np.mean([rollout(bc, test)[1] for _ in range(200)]):.3f}")
data, pol = list(demos), bc
for it in range(1, 6):                                                   # DAgger iterations
    for _ in range(5):
        xs, _ = rollout(pol, rng); data += [(x, expert(x)) for x in xs]   # expert labels learner's states
    pol = fit(data)
    print(f"DAgger iteration {it}: off-road fraction = {np.mean([rollout(pol, test)[1] for _ in range(200)]):.3f}, labelled states = {len(data)}")
print(f"expert:  off-road fraction = {np.mean([rollout(expert, test)[1] for _ in range(200)]):.3f}")

code.title: Lagrangian safe RL and joint-action growth
code.explain: Primal–dual optimisation of a softmax policy on a constrained bandit (budget 0.3), printing reward, cost and λ over time; then mⁿ for several multi-agent settings.
mistakes: Reporting only the final policy and hiding violations during learning.
code.notes: The solution sits exactly at the budget; early iterations violate it.
code.code:
"""Constrained (safe) RL with a Lagrange multiplier, and the joint-action explosion in multi-agent RL.

Safe bandit: 3 actions with mean reward R and mean cost C. Maximise E[R] subject to E[C] <= d.
Policy = softmax over preferences; Lagrangian L = E[R] - lambda (E[C] - d);
policy ascends L, lambda ascends on the constraint violation (projected to >= 0).
"""
import numpy as np
R = np.array([1.0, 0.6, 0.2]); C = np.array([0.9, 0.3, 0.0]); d = 0.3
th, lam = np.zeros(3), 0.0
for t in range(20000):
    pi = np.exp(th - th.max()); pi /= pi.sum()
    adv = (R - lam * C) - pi @ (R - lam * C)
    th += 0.05 * pi * adv * 10                              # exact policy gradient of L for a softmax bandit
    lam = max(0.0, lam + 0.01 * (pi @ C - d))               # dual ascent on the constraint
    if t in (0, 100, 1000, 19999):
        print(f"step {t:>5}: pi = {np.round(pi, 3)}, E[R] = {pi @ R:.3f}, E[C] = {pi @ C:.3f} (budget {d}), lambda = {lam:.3f}")
print("Unconstrained optimum: always action 0 (R = 1.0, C = 0.9) violates the budget. Early on the policy")
print("chases reward and violates the constraint until lambda grows; it settles on action 1 (R = 0.6, C = 0.3),")
print("exactly at the budget, which is the true constrained optimum (mixing actions 0 and 2 would give only 0.47).")

print("\nJoint actions in multi-agent RL: m actions per agent, n agents -> m^n joint actions")
for m, n in ((5, 2), (5, 4), (5, 8), (10, 10)):
    print(f"  m={m:>2}, n={n:>2}: {m ** n:,}")
